title: The "Why This Could Matter" T-Chart (Valued Within Exercise)
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart introduces Valued Within exercises as the more powerful counterpart to teacher-led Mini-Sermons, and walks through the flagship example: the Utility-Value T-Chart, based on Hulleman et al.'s research-backed intervention. Students list personal values in one column and course content or skills in another, then draw connections between the two and write short reflections on why a given connection could matter to their own life. He explains his classroom facilitation process, including using Think-Pair-Share for struggling students and requiring at least five items per column before moving on. He cites the underlying research, noting that when repeated roughly monthly across a school year, the intervention has been shown to improve grades, exam scores, and self-reported course interest, with effects persisting beyond the year it was used.
points: The T-Chart activity is grounded in a named, citable research base (Hulleman et al.'s utility-value intervention, discussed in the Handbook of Wise Interventions), giving it stronger evidentiary weight than most classroom tips.
Stuart provides the exact multi-step procedure and sentence templates, making the activity directly replicable rather than just conceptually described.
He specifies an operational threshold -- at least five items per column before moving to the next step -- as a concrete quality-control rule for the activity's success.
The cited research shows effects (grades, exam scores, self-reported interest) persisting beyond the year of the intervention when repeated monthly, elevating the exercise's stakes.
quotes: A Valued Within exercise is simple: Any time you have students articulate (via writing or speaking) why the work of learning is valuable, that's a Valued Within exercise.

On one side (Column A), they write down a list of things they value: hobbies, interests, goals, character attributes. On the other side (Column B), they write a list of things they have learned or done in class.
I pose it as a problem, like this: "Most people can't connect the things they do in school with the values they have outside of school. I believe that you can do this.

For this exercise to work, you really need students to be successful at each step before moving on. As you guide students through each step, you want to be circulating and checking to see their progress. Once students have five items or more per column, that's when you move on.

What's amazing about this exercise is that, when repeated roughly once per month over the course of the school year, researchers find significant improvements in things like grades, final exam scores, and self-reported interest in the course, and this difference continues beyond the year of the intervention.
